Chapter Four: The Making of Fear – How Security Forces Control Society
In Syria, fear isn’t just something you feel every now and then. It’s a way of life. The security agencies there don’t just watch people from a distance—they create an entire atmosphere of suspicion and doubt. It’s like everyone’s living under this constant cloud, never quite sure who’s watching or listening.
Imagine this for a second: talking about politics, or just sharing your thoughts, suddenly feels risky. Even inside your own home, conversations get quieter, just in case there’s someone—somewhere—listening in.
One evening, a group of neighbors gathered at someone’s house to watch a soccer match. At first, the mood was light and everyone was having fun. But as soon as the topic drifted toward politics, the whole room fell silent. Faces changed. Someone glanced nervously at the window, as if they expected eyes on them at any moment. In that instant, it hit everyone—fear had woven itself into the tiniest details of their daily lives.
And it’s not just about obvious surveillance. The security forces rely on a wide network of informants. In every neighborhood, there’s always someone passing along information—sometimes out of fear, sometimes hoping for favors, and sometimes even out of spite.
There’s a story about a young man who worked at a small shop. He was forced into helping the security services after they threatened his job. He never wanted to hurt anyone, but he felt trapped—so he started reporting on his coworkers and neighbors. The guilt built up over time, but he just couldn’t see a way out.
Fear seeps into institutions too. Take schools and universities—there’s always someone keeping an eye on students and teachers. One teacher noticed that a usually outspoken student had suddenly become quiet in class. When he asked why, the student simply said he didn’t want his words to be misunderstood. That kind of extreme caution? It’s become the norm. People would rather stay silent than risk saying the wrong thing.
Even at social events, fear is right there in the room. At a wedding, for example, a guest tried to share a political joke. But as soon as he did, people stopped laughing. Someone quietly warned him, “Be careful—not everyone here is family.” In that moment, it was clear: fear had become stronger than joy. Everyone was on edge, always alert.
And here’s something to pay attention to—this atmosphere isn’t just crafted by the security agencies alone. Sometimes, the community plays along—consciously or not. Many people try to justify their cooperation by saying they’re just trying to protect themselves. But in the end, it leads to a society where suspicion is everywhere, and trust is nowhere to be found.
Over time, fear turns into a daily habit. Picture this: an intelligence officer sits down with an old friend. They reminisce about their childhood, but the friend now chooses every word so carefully, avoiding anything that might sound risky. That’s when the officer realizes—fear has built a wall between them, and life will never be the same.
So, that’s how security forces manage to create an atmosphere of constant fear. It doesn’t just affect individuals—it seeps into every part of life, making suspicion the norm, and reshaping how an entire society lives and connects.
